catalog_quote: Hixkaryana (Derbyshire 1979) is a language of the Cariban family, and is spoken in the Amazon (northern Brazil). It has no distinctive vowel length — all surface length reflects rhythmic organization, or so-called ‘rhythmic lengthening’. ... The generalization that governs the lengthening pattern is the following: in words of three or more syllables, every even-numbered non-final open syllable is stressed, and its vowel is lengthened. This alternating length pattern can be characterized as ‘iambic’ ... final syllables in Hixkaryana never undergo vowel lengthening, and are never stressed. ... Turning now from open syllables to closed syllables, we find that these are always stressed, but that their vowels never lengthen. Even though closed syllables fail to undergo lengthening themselves, they do affect the lengthening pattern of open syllables, serving as reference points in counting sy…
sweep_summary: Both title-works with stress in the title for Hixkaryana were already held by the project and were read in full this search of works with stress in the title. (1) Halle & Idsardi 2000 (TLR 17, author-hosted open scan, scanned) is a rule-based re-analysis of Kager 1999's Hixkaryana data: final vowel never stressed, heavy (closed) syllables always stressed and foot-closing, iterative binary right-headed footing from the left, stressed open syllables lengthen; it adds that monosyllabic closed words yoh/kay/min (Derbyshire 1985:17,23,28) are stressed; it is silent on primary vs secondary stress. Confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding. (2) Hagberg 2006 (SIL e-Books 3, open PDF; = 1993 Arizona diss.) uses Hixkaryana (data after Derbyshire 1985/Hayes 1991) as the exemplar of the iambic foot: final syllable extrametrical, iambic feet L-to-R, stress to the heavy member, open-vowel lengthening; fn.96 (p.100) states that all stresses but one are secondary and primary stress is set by intonation. Confirms. Neither is first-hand, and neither adds anything beyond the catalog's existing Kager/Hayes chain. The best first-hand statement in the directory remains Derbyshire 1999 'Carib' p.28 (Dixon & Aikhenvald, open archive.org text): 'In HI, primary stress occurs on final or penultimate syllables, varying according to the dialect; secondary stress occurs on heavy syllables, i.e., those with final C or (prosodic) long vowels' - which should replace Kager 1999 as the deciding source for the primary-stress rule while leaving classification weight unchanged. Still unheld: Derbyshire 1979 (LDS 1) and Derbyshire 1985 pp.175-182 (SIL PL 76; archive.org print-disabled only), Hayes 1995:205-208. discovery by Crossref, archive.org and direct URL probes.

new_statements.quote: Stress, to my knowledge, is contrastive only in PA. It is predictable in terms of syllable structure for some languages: in CA, it occurs on any second heavy syllable (one with a long vowel, diphthong, or final C) counting from the left; otherwise on the final syllable (Hoff 1992). ... In HI, primary stress occurs on final or penultimate syllables, varying according to the dialect; secondary stress occurs on heavy syllables, i.e., those with final C or (prosodic) long vowels. [note 3, p.29:] In other languages there is prosodic lengthening of vowels in CV syllables, predictable in terms of the syllable patterning in words and phrases (CA, HI ...).

new_statements.reading: The primary describer himself: Hixkaryana stress is non-contrastive; primary stress is at the right edge (final or penultimate, by dialect); secondary stress falls on heavy syllables, heavy = CVC or prosodically lengthened CV. This is a first-hand statement, unlike Kager 1999 (a textbook restatement of Derbyshire 1979 via Hayes 1995) and the two works with stress in the title (both theoretical re-analyses of Derbyshire 1985 data). It confirms the weight coding (CVC heavy; rhythmic lengthening; closed syllables stressed) and supplies a citable primary-stress placement (final/penult, dialectal) that the catalog currently carries only through Hayes 1995:206-207 ('main stress.. depends on the intonation pattern'). Neither Halle-Idsardi 2000 nor Hagberg 2006 mentions primary-stress placement except Hagberg's fn.96, which repeats the Derbyshire 1985/Hayes 1991 intonation account.

sources.quote: p.11: 'Stress in Hixkaryana occurs on closed syllables and on the nonfinal even members of a string of open syllables. Stressed vowels in open syllables are lengthened, but there are no instances of underlying vowel length.' p.101 (175): 'Hixkaryana Stress Assignment: a. Make the final syllable extrametrical. b. Construct iambic feet iteratively from left to right. c. Insert * into each foot and link.' fn.96, p.100: 'Notice that all stresses are written as primary. In fact, both Derbyshire (1985) and Hayes (1991) state that all of a word's stresses except one are secondary, and that primary stress is determined not by metrical structure but by intonation.'

sources.note: General theory of stress that uses Hixkaryana (data after Derbyshire 1985 and Hayes 1991, in Derbyshire's practical orthography) as its exemplar of the right-headed asymmetric (iambic) foot: final syllable extrametrical, iambic feet built left-to-right, stress links to the heavy (right) member, stressed open vowels lengthen; a lone light syllable cannot form a degenerate foot (tohkurye:hona, not *tohkurye:ho:na). De vez em quando ocorrem tambem em certas unidades ritmicas e nestes casos a duracao da vogal e quase sempre mais longa do que em outros casos. Duracao mais longa denota enfase.' (stress and length non-phonemic, phonologically conditioned; no rule stated).
